title: 1 Introduction
use_cases: Use when developing formal methods to evaluate AI-generated storytelling content
Implement when benchmarking machine-told stories against human narrative nuances
Configure when quantifying storytelling devices like novelty and surprise in media corpora
Use when building tools for machine learning scientists to analyze multi-modal narrative structures
content:
As AI systems begin to tell their own stories [1, 2], it becomes crucial to develop formal methods for understanding and evaluating the content they produce [3, 4, 5, 6]. We introduce a general information-theoretic framework to measure narratives, capturing key storytelling elements like novelty and surprise [7, 8, 9]. This work provides tools for creatives and for applied machine learning scientists to analyse narrative structures and for GenAI researchers to benchmark stories told by machines. It thereby also offers a foundation for developing human-in-the-loop AI systems assisting in narrative creation while maintaining the nuanced human understanding of stories [10].

Narratives represent a key higher-level representation of how a story gets told [3] and are crucial to how we understand worlds, both fictional and real. Previous machine learning work on detecting narratives has focussed on specific content and modalities [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. We build on this by introducing a general information-theoretic narrative framework that is agnostic to content and modality and lets us intuitively capture crucial storytelling devices, like novelty and surprise – which have thus far seen less attention in the study of narratives. We illustrate our measures in a corpus of over 3000 minutes of TV shows, one of the most popular forms of contemporary storytelling.
